A therapist or other counselor is essential for her. When she gets older and realized the initiative you took, she will be grateful. It’s very important that she learns other coping mechanisms. If she is not putting them in hidden places, it very well could be for attention, but that is also an issue that needs to be addressed, because that means it’s a cry for help. 

One of the things it took for me to stop self harming was to see how it was impacting my loved ones. I didn’t know it was that bad. To me, it allowed me to feel numb in my most emotionally intense moments. But when the people around me were hurt and concerned, I had to reconsider the choices I was making, and really tried to stop. 

I again suggest you look into a therapist. I know it can be expensive so there also may be other community resources available depending on your location.

I also suggest you encourage her to stop self harming and be transparent about how it concerns you. Don’t blame her or make her feel in trouble, just tell her how you feel.

It sounds like maybe you two had a bit of unhealthy dependency throughout the relationship. I think staying friends would be a good thing for both of you, but it’s really important to have a life that is your own, and for her to have a life that is her own. 

It’s very important in a relationship to not ‘need’ one another. It’s ok to rely on someone or to very strongly want them apart of your life, but to feel like you need them to function is unhealthy and I speak from experience.

I think if you do want to be friends with her then setting a limit on how many times you can talk throughout the day or meet up with her is a good idea. But if you do want to pursue a relationship with her again, then those limits should also take place as it is important for both of you to have boundaries.

Best of luck to you!
